stem.text: A function g has derivative \( g'(x) = 6\left(x + 2\right)\left(x - 2\right) \). Using the second derivative test where it applies, determine whether g has a relative maximum, a relative minimum, or neither at \( x = -2 \) and at \( x = -5 \).

answer_key.label: At \( x = -2 \), g has a relative maximum because \( g'(-2) = 0 \) and \( g''(-2) = -24 < 0 \); at \( x = -5 \), g has no relative extremum because \( g'(-5) = 126 \ne 0 \).

worked_solution.text: \( g'(-2) = 0 \), so \( x = -2 \) is a critical point, while \( g'(-5) = 126 \ne 0 \), so \( x = -5 \) is not.
worked_solution.rule_named: critical points are zeros of the first derivative
second derivative evaluated at the critical point

worked_solution.text: By the second derivative test g has a relative maximum at \( x = -2 \). At \( x = -5 \) the first derivative is not zero, so g has no relative extremum there and the test does not apply.

options.label: At \( x = -2 \), g has a relative minimum because \( g'(-2) = 0 \) and \( g''(-2) = -24 < 0 \); at \( x = -5 \), g has no relative extremum because \( g'(-5) = 126 \ne 0 \).
options.derivation: the sign convention of the test reversed, so a negative second derivative is read as a minimum and a positive one as a maximum

options.derivation: the relative extremum from the second derivative test extended to an absolute one with no argument that it is the only critical point, which it is not
